silo_relevance: This paper is relevant to simulation_monte_carlo because it targets the state-preparation bottleneck that often dominates quantum Monte Carlo workflows, and it provides a distribution-loading circuit designed to feed amplitude-estimation-style simulation pipelines more efficiently (C-001, C-012, C-035). Its most silo-specific value is the claim that static, parameter-efficient loading can reduce repeated preprocessing and support empirical distribution approximation for risk quantities derived from simulated data (C-009, C-023, C-040).

key_points.point: Addresses the input/state-preparation bottleneck that limits quantum Monte Carlo pipelines.
key_points.silo_note: Simulation Monte Carlo methods need efficient loading of probability distributions into quantum states before estimation; this paper is directly about that bottleneck.

key_points.point: Provides a maximum-entropy distribution loader that prepares probability distributions in a form suitable for downstream estimation.
key_points.silo_note: For Monte Carlo-style simulation, the key issue is preparing the target distribution efficiently enough to make repeated sampling/estimation practical.

key_points.point: Claims reduced end-to-end resource cost by keeping the circuit static and updating only O(M) parameters.
key_points.silo_note: Monte Carlo workflows often require repeated re-evaluation as model parameters change; a static, reusable loader is especially relevant when many simulation runs are needed.

key_points.point: Connects directly to quantum Monte Carlo / amplitude-estimation-style finance workflows and sensitivity estimation.
key_points.silo_note: This is the closest match to simulation_monte_carlo because it frames the loader as part of QMCI and supports derivative/sensitivity calculations that commonly accompany Monte Carlo simulation.

key_points.point: Shows empirical distribution approximation and VaR recovery from simulated data using slowly varying observables as constraints.
key_points.silo_note: This is especially relevant to Monte Carlo simulation because it demonstrates fitting an empirical distribution from simulated samples and extracting a risk statistic from that approximation.
